entry.title: Here's How I Learned to Love Calculus (And You Can Too!)
entry.content:
Foreword

Something I wish they emphasized more in math courses is how the different years of classes actually come together, and why it actually matters.

No I'm not going to get into the debate of, "Oh why do we even need math?!" and other such things you might say sitting in that absolutely mind-numbingly boring and pointless math class. I'm not going to sit here and blow smoke up your ass, spouting such refrains as, "Hey, you can calculate the perimeter of your yard!" because we all know that's not why we learn math.

The better reason they tell us is that the act of learning and understanding strictly logical concepts helps build abstract thought. That, I can get behind, but we shouldn't do our students the disservice of teaching them relatively disjoint concepts that only mesh together when the two units overlap.

I also won't be going into the, you know, whole education system. I will leave this point here: The best kind of learning is led by the learner's own curiosity. Sure, it's kinda obvious when I say it like that, but humans are naturally curious creatures. Our brains strive to learn, to grow, to adapt, etc.; when we are genuinely intrigued, we desire an answer, an explanation that actually satisfies us. I may be-well, I am-biased. I love math, so naturally I feel this curiosity should be shared.

That being said, not everyone is genuinely interested in math, and even if we taught it how I truly wish we could teach it, they might just not really care. That's okay! It's important to have a diverse society! It's fine (and good!) that we have people who just don't want to live in the world of the abstract, we need people to focus on what truly drives them. Math ain't that for some (a lot) of people, but I'll still argue that, just as the liberal arts are arguably important for everyone (that's an essay for another time), math should remain a subject we throw onto students because it is useful for those reasons that math teacher who wishes their students gave a damn used to tell us after all.

Anywho, my issue is with how we learn it, so I'm going to just start ranting about how you can get to calculus, trigonometry, and all that jazz from basic physics principles.

Let's Get the Ball Rolling

No, literally.

Let's talk about movement, any shape suffices but let's imagine a ball as we tend to have the intuition that a rolling ball rolls like a ball rolls ball the ball roll.

This ball right here isn't moving. It's just sitting there, doing nothing. And it's gonna keep doing nothing, right? I have to do something to the ball to get it moving; I have to apply a force. So I give this ball a shove and...it just keeps rolling. And (assuming there is no friction and the abstract scene we have built is physically perfect), it will just keep on rolling until I do something to stop the ball rolling; I have to apply a for-well, yeah, you get the picture. Another force is needed to change the ball's movement. w To restate what we've concluded so far, the speed (& direction), or the velocity, of the ball remain(s) the same until a force is applied. So, for now, just think of a force as a change in velocity. Wow, we've learned Newton's first law. Great job everyone!

Let's continue our joyous journey by imagining this ball just carying along at some speed. How about 1 meter per second. That's easy to think about. During the span of 1 second, the ball will move 1 meter. Cool! How about 5 seconds? That's easy, 5 meters! We intuitively know that $$ 1 \frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}} \times 5 \text{s} = 5 \text{m} $$
